Assignment 7-1: In three or four typed pages, describe your family background in regard to cultural influences. Discuss as well as you can both your mother (and her family) and your father (and his family). Include any other families who may have influenced you as well. For each, discuss attitudes and views toward religion, family, work, education, and wealth. Describe the socioeconomic location of your family and its religious context. Also, how do members of your family tend to relate to each other? Does your family tend to be warm and “huggy” or cold and distant? Finally, try to relate your family background to your own set of values and outlooks. What have you retained? What have you rejected?

*Note: This assignment is not meant to pry into your personal life. Feel free to omit anything in the written assignment about which you are sensitive. But be sure to think about those things you omit so that you are aware of their influence on your study of the Bible. This exercise is a self-analysis; it is for your benefit and not outs.*
_________________________________________________________________________

**Family Background and Cultural Influences**

I was born into a Singaporean family with both parents being ethnically Chinese (FYI, Singaporean Chinese have a distinct identity separate from mainland Chinese, which means our loyalty lies with Singapore, and not China! Just a fun fact). The typical Singaporean Chinese family embodies a meritocratic mindset, where hard work is essential for survival. This societal culture is reflected in the achievements of our local students, who frequently excel in global competitions in mathematics, science, and more. Many of our behaviors and values stem from this spirit of perseverance and dedication. By and large, the typical Singaporean parent prioritizes securing the best education for their child. If having religious friends broadens their horizons and helps them become well-rounded, that’s seen as positive. However, if religious commitments, like attending services on Sunday, take time away from studying, that’s viewed negatively. This mindset is pervasive even within church communities, where some parents allow their children to skip church if they have a big exam coming up.

Singaporean culture is quite sensitive when it comes to religion, and people often avoid asking religious questions for fear of potentially offending others. With four main religions—Islam, Buddhism, Christianity, and Hinduism—coexisting in our society, there's an unspoken rule to tread carefully around matters of faith.

My father’s family consisted of his three younger brothers and a younger sister. They were raised in a Buddhist household, but my dad became a Christian during his teenage years. As a result, his siblings were exposed to Christian practices and became somewhat knowledgeable about them. Occasionally, they would show curiosity and ask questions, but these conversations were usually brief and cautious, reflecting the general sensitivity around religious topics. From my perspective as a young child, nothing substantial came from these exchanges.

On my mother’s side, she also came from a middle-income family. Her siblings have all done well financially, and some converted to Christianity, though not from the church of Christ heritage. However, religion wasn’t a central part of their identity, so it didn’t dominate conversations. Discussions typically focused on secular achievements and milestones. Occasionally, “Christian matters” would surface, especially when societal norms clashed with our Christian beliefs—like in discussions about drinking alcohol, offering joss sticks to the deceased, or attending family gatherings on Sundays. But for the most part, these conversations were rare and handled with cautious grace.

Growing up, my immediate family was in what you might call an "upper-poor" income bracket. We had a home and a roof over our heads, though simple. We had food, clothes, and entertainment, but just the bare minimum, often from gifts from friends and family. There were many reasons for this, but the largest was due to the cancer that took my mother’s life when I was four. The treatment was long and extremely costly, and I’m sure it took a large toll on my dad’s health and time as he cared for her while providing for the family. Nevertheless, my father’s and mother’s siblings were always supportive, often giving us small gifts of money and helping to look after us.

Unlike many Chinese families in Singapore, we primarily spoke English at home. This was largely due to my father's upbringing and his deep involvement in the church, which was an English-speaking community. His Chinese wasn’t great, and this shaped the language environment in our household, which then trickled down to us. So while I’m Chinese, I am quite different from the kind of “Chinese” most people would think of.

**Religious Context and Family Values**

Both of my parents were Christians, having converted from a predominantly Buddhist society. They faced a lot of pressure and rejection from their own parents—some were even locked out of their house for attending church on Sundays. Naturally, those who remained faithful in Christ became “battle-hardened” warriors who had fought tirelessly for their faith and, through God’s providence, emerged victorious. My parents were no exception. This tenacity forged the spirit by which they served Christ and their own family. I remember many anecdotes of how their parents would cut up all their clothes so that they had nothing to wear for church, leading them to wear their school uniforms instead. Or how their parents would threaten them, saying that if they continued to follow Jesus, they would no longer be their sons or daughters. But by God’s grace, and after 20 to 30 years of persistent faith and effort, most of them saw the change in their lives and eventually decided to follow Jesus.

My father studied at Four Seas Bible College in Singapore and was trained to be a preacher. He was sent to start a congregation in Punggol, a region located in the northeastern part of Singapore. The congregation grew to about 20+ people, but due to a falling out with an American missionary, the church eventually dwindled to solely my family. Despite this, my father remained committed to the mission, continuing to serve faithfully in his ministry to this day. This was the kind of man I lived under and the kind of values that were instilled in our family by example. My mother retired from her job as an accountant to focus on the household. Part of that was practical, with four kids to care for, but it was also to ensure our home was rooted in Christian principles.

1. Select keywords.
2. Think of all adjacent words that comes to your mind
3. Go wikipedia and explore and see whether there're concepts you're interested in
4. Check out the sources of articles because that's where you'll find similar content
5. Come up with a research question and refine it as such:
	1. # Research Question Development  

### Write a Research Question  
**Example:**  
> *What is the effect of high school civics classes on first-time voting behavior?*  

**Your Research Question:**  
> *How have different theological understandings and practices of baptism across various Christian traditions shaped their broader understanding of God?*  

---

### How is your question focused?  
**Example:**  
> *My research question focuses on how one class (civics) affects one group (first-time voters).*  

**Your Focus:**  
> *My research question focuses on the visible theological distinctness that arises from a group's understanding of Baptism.*  

---

### How is your question analyzable?  
**Example:**  
> *It is more than a yes or no question, which means I can make conclusions or recommendations based on my research. Maybe I’ll find that civics classes increase voter turnout and be able to argue that all high schools should offer them.*  

**Your Analysis:**  
> *It's more than a yes/no question. I can make conclusions and showcase the strengths and weaknesses of each view. This may help us understand what unifying points all groups have to stand on together, as well as the weaknesses of their perspectives for their consideration.*  

---

### How is your question interpretable?  
**Example:**  
> *My question lets me see if there is a relationship between civics classes and first-time voters, like if people are more likely to vote a certain way if they have had a civics class.*  

**Your Interpretation:**  
> *My question lets me see how each group thinks and why they think that way. This will help me better empathize with their views and see what is biblical and godly about them, which may help inform my tradition.*  

---

### Can you answer your question in the time/space/length required? Why?  
**Example:**  
> *The topic isn’t too broad or too narrow, so it can fill a five-page paper.*  

**Your Answer:**  
> *The topic can go very deep and broad—it could take up an entire thesis. However, it could also be explored more generally, perhaps within a ten-page paper.*  

### Confirmation Bias
How to fight against it:
First, seek out the other side. It’s really hard to do, and takes time, but find and read sources that challenge your thinking. Look for quality information, though—seeking out a different opinion is only useful if that opinion is credible and grounded in reality. This strategy is especially useful for writing or research projects. What you learn about opposing opinions will strengthen and refine your own opinion, which makes your writing stronger and more convincing.  

Second, pop your filter bubble. Social media feeds are confirmation bias (and fake news) gold mines! Your feeds are full of things you already agree with, but that doesn’t mean they’re accurate, true, or the whole story. Before you like or share something, do some lateral reading. To learn how, check out the Niche Academy Lateral Reading tutorial. Make this a habit, especially if you agree with what you’re reading. 

Finally, debate with yourself. Before continuing that argument with your friend, argue with yourself about whether plants have feelings. This will improve your research and writing by exploring arguments and counter-arguments before broadcasting them to the world. Think about what you believe, why you believe it, and if there is any room for additional information. You don’t have to convince yourself, but you’re less likely to fall into confirmation bias thinking if you take time to question what you don’t know, and—more importantly—what you do know.

### False Equivalencies
I had this when I wanted to believe that Baptism was necessary for salvation. So every verse that showed Baptism and salvation together, I would equate baptism to salvation.

Do Lateral reading - Understand who is writing, how they get funded, what's their goal. What do other people have to say about them

### How to fight strawman arguments
- Restate their original clearly and accurately
- Make sure others agree with the point
- Acknowledge the good points they make
- Focus on the main idea

### How to be productive and not strawman people
- Get as much information about a topic as you can
- Learn about opposing ideas from people who hold them
- Focus on finding the strongest part of an opposing idea!
- Respect the opposing idea and the people who hold it

One of the two spies that trusted in God's ability to lead the nation of Israel into the promised Land. [[Num 14]]
Was the leader that took over from Moses to lead them. ([[Deu 31_1-8]], [[Deu 34_9]])

**Meaning of the word**
'Joshua') in later books of the Hebrew Bible and among Jews of the Second Temple period. The name corresponds to the Greek spelling Iesous (Ἰησοῦς), from which, through the Latin IESVS/Iesus, comes the English spelling Jesus.

_Yeshua_ is the Hebrew name, and its English spelling is “Joshua.” _Iesous_ is the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew name, and its English spelling is “Jesus.” Thus, the names “Joshua” and “Jesus” are essentially the same; both are English pronunciations of the Hebrew and Greek names for our Lord. (For examples of how the two names are interchangeable, see [Acts 7:45](https://www.bibleref.com/Acts/7/Acts-7-45.html) and [Hebrews 4:8](https://www.bibleref.com/Hebrews/4/Hebrews-4-8.html) in the KJV. In both cases, the word _Jesus_ refers to the Old Testament character Joshua.)

**Significance**
Joshua led Israel to promised land -> Jesus leads the world to heaven.

# Obsidian Knowledge Base
Welcome to my Obsidian Knowledge Base! This guide is designed to help you access and explore my thoughts, as well as contribute if you'd like.

# Setup 
### Just to View

1. **Download Obsidian**: Visit the [Obsidian download page](https://obsidian.md/download) and download the application for your operating system.
2. **Open Obsidian**: Install and open Obsidian on your device.
3. **Clone the Knowledge Base**:
    - Use GitHub Desktop or any Git client to clone the repository, or simply download the repository as a ZIP file from the GitHub page.
	    - If using GitHub Desktop, select "Clone a repository" and enter the repository URL: `https://github.com/AlphaeusNg/ObsidianKB.git`.
	    - If downloading as a ZIP, unzip the file to your desired location.
      - ![Screenshot to show zipped file download button](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5e6587f3-4936-4d24-9e10-ea2d680cf0ac)

1. **Open in Obsidian**:
    - In Obsidian, click on "Open folder as vault" and select the cloned or unzipped folder.
    - Explore the notes and enjoy!

### To Contribute

1. **Download Git**: If you don't have Git installed, download it from the [Git website](https://git-scm.com/downloads) and install it.
2. **Clone the Repository**:
    - Open your terminal or Git Bash.
    - Run the following command to clone the repository:      
        `git clone https://github.com/AlphaeusNg/ObsidianKB.git`
    - Navigate into the cloned directory:        
        `cd ObsidianKB`
3. **Create a New Branch**: Create a new branch for your changes.
		`git checkout -b your-branch-name`
1. **Make Your Changes**: Add your notes or edits using Obsidian or your preferred text editor.
2. **Commit and Push Your Changes**:
    - Add the changes to staging:        
        `git add .`
    - Commit your changes:        
        `git commit -m "Description of your changes"`
    - Push your changes to GitHub:
        `git push origin your-branch-name`
6. **Create a Pull Request**:
    - Go to the GitHub repository page.
    - Click on "Compare & pull request."
    - Provide a clear description of your changes and submit the pull request.

Thank you for contributing or taking the time to explore my knowledge base!

The essentiality of Baptism required for [[Salvation]] hinges on the interpretation of these verses:
- For -> [[Acts 2_38]], [[Acts 22_16]], [[Mark 16_16]], [[1 Peter 3_20-21]], [[John 3_5]], [[Gal 3_27]]
- "Against" -> [[John 3_16]], [[Acts 16_31]], [[Eph 2_8-9]], [[Eph 5_25-27]]
	- Not necessarily contradicts Baptism, but more of the idea that [[Belief]] or [[Faith]] in Christ is the axiom for salvation, and Baptism fits into that framework via being an "outward sign of an inward faith" [[Rom 4]] of the parallel to Abraham's justification. Therefore salvation occurs at belief rather than baptism.
	- [[Eph 5_25-27]]: 25 Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, 26 that he might **sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word**, 27 so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.
		- The "washing of water" with the word is the *thing* that cleanses her unto sanctification (set apart, holy). Water more of a symbol of cleansing rather than the link to baptism?

### Seems to not be considered a literal part in the [[Gospel]]
When I read [[1 Cor 1]], I was surprised to find out 2 things of how Paul views Baptism in v14-16:
	*14 I thank God that ==I baptized none of you== except Crispus and Gaius, 15 so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. 16 (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.) 17 For ==Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel==, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.*
1. He separates Baptism from the [[Gospel]]. If the Gospel is the power of Salvation to those who believe ([[Rom 1_16]]), and Baptism is a necessary component of that, Paul would be contradicting himself by not fulfilling that requirement.
	1. Granted we recognize that the point Paul was making was in addressing the divisions that arose in Corinthians and Paul was glad that by not baptizing them, he reduced one source of division, yet there is still valid theological implications of his statements.
2. If Baptism is to be understood as *essential* for salvation, Paul is literally saying:
	*14 I thank God that ==I <u>saved</u> none of you== except Crispus and Gaius, 15 so that no one may say that you were <u>saved</u> in my name. 16 (I did <u>save</u> also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I <u>saved</u> anyone else.) 17 For ==Christ did not send me to <u>save</u> but to preach the gospel==, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.*

While Baptism does have a "strong salvific scent" due to what Jesus commands in [[Matt 28]] and the other verses above that seems to tie salvation directly to it, perhaps the most faithful and biblical way to understand it is that it occurs as a *result* of saving faith rather than the *thing* that saves. What this also means is that, in my current understanding (5/2/2025), if a believer does not desire to be baptized, I would question the genuineness of said faith.

**Helpful Traditions vs. Unhelpful Principles in the Church of Christ Heritage: A Biblical and Pastoral Examination**

## Introduction

The Church of Christ (COC) has a rich heritage rooted in a desire for biblical faithfulness, simple Christianity, and unity based on Scripture. Many within the movement sincerely seek to honor God by following the Bible as their only authority. However, any theological tradition—including COC—must be examined in light of Scripture to discern which elements are helpful and which might hinder a fuller understanding of God's truth. This paper provides a pastoral and biblical evaluation of COC ecclesiology and hermeneutics, affirming its strengths while addressing areas that may require reevaluation for greater faithfulness to Christ.

---

## **Helpful Traditions in the Church of Christ Heritage**

### **1. Emphasis on Biblical Authority**

- The COC has a strong commitment to following Scripture, which is commendable (2 Tim 3:16-17).
    
- The movement seeks to avoid human traditions that obscure biblical teaching (Mark 7:6-8).
    
- The intent to restore New Testament Christianity reflects a noble desire for faithfulness (Acts 2:42).
    

### **2. Focus on Congregational Autonomy**

- The COC upholds local church independence, which has biblical precedent (Acts 14:23; Phil 1:1).
    
- This autonomy protects against hierarchical abuses and ensures accountability within the local body (1 Pet 5:1-4).
    

### **3. Commitment to Baptism and the Lord’s Supper**

- The emphasis on baptism aligns with the biblical model (Acts 2:38; Rom 6:3-4).
    
- Weekly observance of the Lord’s Supper fosters remembrance of Christ’s sacrifice (1 Cor 11:23-26).
    

### **4. Simplicity in Worship and Church Life**

- Worship in the COC is generally free from excessive formalism, focusing on devotion to God (John 4:24).
    
- A cappella singing encourages congregational participation and unity in worship (Eph 5:19; Col 3:16).
    

---

## **Unhelpful Principles in the Church of Christ Heritage**

### **1. The Overuse of the “Silence of Scripture” Argument**

- The COC often applies the principle that “silence prohibits” rather than “silence permits.”
    
- This approach is not consistently applied in Scripture itself. For example:
    
    - Hebrews 7:14 states that Jesus was not from Levi, but the text does not prohibit a non-Levite from being a priest; rather, it reveals God's sovereign choice.
        
    - The Bible does not explicitly authorize **meeting in church buildings**, yet this practice is accepted.
        
- A more biblical approach would be **to allow silence where Scripture does** and focus on positive instruction rather than assumed prohibitions ([[Col 3_17]]).
    

### **2. A Strict Patternism That Misses the Heart of Worship**

- While seeking to restore the New Testament church is admirable, **hyper-patternism** can become restrictive.
    
- Scripture provides principles rather than rigid blueprints for church function (Acts 2:42; 1 Cor 14:40).
    
- Worship elements such as instrumental music or multiple cups in communion should not be elevated to tests of faithfulness (Rom 14:1-5).
    

### **3. Theological Isolation and Rejection of Broader Christian History**

- The COC sometimes distances itself from the larger body of Christ, neglecting valuable insights from church history (Eph 4:4-6).
    
- Early church writings (e.g., Augustine, Chrysostom) provide helpful perspectives on Scripture that should not be dismissed outright.
    

### **4. Tendency Toward Sectarianism and Exclusivism**

- The belief that the COC is the “one true church” can create division and contradict the unity Christ desires (John 17:20-21).
    
- There are faithful believers outside the COC, as seen in the broader kingdom of God (1 Cor 12:12-13).
    
- A more biblical approach embraces unity with all who hold to the gospel (Eph 4:3-6).
    

---

## **Moving Toward a More Biblical Faithfulness**

### **A More Consistent Hermeneutic**

- Instead of **command, example, and necessary inference**, a **Christ-centered hermeneutic** should be used (Luke 24:27; 2 Cor 3:6).
    
- Contextual interpretation allows for better application of Scripture (Nehemiah 8:8).
    

### **Balancing Restoration with Grace**

- The goal should not be to perfectly replicate first-century Christianity, but to **follow Christ faithfully in every generation** (Matt 28:19-20).
    
- A more biblical emphasis on **grace and faith** can help avoid legalism (Eph 2:8-9).
    

---

## **Conclusion**

The Church of Christ has a heritage that emphasizes biblical authority, congregational autonomy, baptism, and simple worship. These are commendable principles. However, some of its hermeneutical and ecclesiological approaches—particularly regarding the silence of Scripture, rigid patternism, theological isolation, and sectarian tendencies—need careful reexamination. By embracing a broader biblical framework centered on Christ and the gospel, the COC can remain faithful to Scripture while fostering greater unity and faithfulness to Jesus.

MN502 Biblical Preaching Assignment 

I really enjoyed the various dimensions Steve brings about regarding the Calling of a Preacher.

1. First and foremost, the preacher **owes it to those supporting him**. Even from a worldly perspective, it's a rudimentary principle that's reasonable to see. The preacher does a good work for the Lord, in labouring for the growth of the body, and the body, in turn, supplies what is within their means for the benefit of the preacher. This relationship is good and glorifies God. Yet, if the preacher grows lazy, he tarnishes the godly relationship established between him and the church, and he betrays the sacrifice the body makes for him. Folly and ingratitude is returned for sacrificial love!  
    1 Tim 5:18 says,
    
    > For the Scripture says, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain,” and, “The laborer deserves his wages."
    
    A worker is worth his wages **if** he "treads out the grain"! So at the minimum, be worthy of your wages!  
    
2. The idea of **being a hindrance** was very apt as well. In our mission for Christ, laziness will be an obvious stumbling block unto others. Even the perception of laziness, whether true or not, gives Satan an easy opportunity to tempt others to sin. Having thoughts like "Oh, he didn't join this event because..." and then Satan swoops in for the kill, "...because he's hard at work elsewhere distracted with idle things!" Furthermore, as Steve pointed out, if we don't "walk the talk," our message loses power, opening the door to contempt for God.  
      
3. **Failure to adequately prepare lessons** is a point that hits closer to my heart. I often struggle to discipline myself to sit down, open up my Google doc, and meditate on the Word. Steve's question, "Do we enter the pulpit because we have to say something, or because we have something to say?" accurately illuminates the spirit with which I've served the body. May God mold and strengthen me in this area in time, all glory be to Him!  
    
4. Recently in my ministry, I've begun seeing with clarity the importance of one-on-one meetups and have begun meeting up more often with the young men and young guys in my church. And so, the **failure to get involved with others** is a tragedy God has opened my eyes to. A big problem with not meeting outside of Sundays is that genuine relationships will not have a platform to grow and mature. These interactions are where bridges are built, problems are shared, sins are confessed, and growth in Jesus our Lord happens. Therefore, a preacher who fails to do this out of laziness is severely letting the congregation down.  
    
5. And perhaps the most fundamental point is this - **fall more deeply in love with Jesus**. Steve hit it right where "We do not consider the difficult work we do for those we love". If preachers are born again (John 3), it's no longer them who live, but Christ who lives in them (Gal 2:20). The deeper we love Jesus, the deeper we will love the congregation, and the deeper all the other points will be addressed. 2 Cor 5:14-15 says:
    
    > 14 For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that one died for all, and therefore all died. 15 And he died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and was raised again.
    
    and so, if we're truly convinced that Jesus has died for us, the love of Christ will **compel** us to live for Jesus who has defeated death on our behalf! Which means putting to death laziness! For that leads to death.

It's not what many of us from COC heritage intuitively understand what the Lord's Supper to be - a necessary ritual that we MUST partake of. Christians SHOULD and OUGHT to desire to partake it.

**Summary**
1. A continuation of the OT's [[Passover]]. Jews remember God's deliverance and now Christians remember Jesus's deliverance. (Luk 22, )
2. Bread
	1. symbolizes body, for remembrance of Jesus. ([[Luk 22_19]])
	2. "Take, eat; this is my body" -> Called to eat it with understanding that this is Jesus's body ([[Mat 26_26]], [[Mark 14_22]])
3. Fruit of the Vine/Cup
	1. 'poured out' -> symbolize the sacrifice and atonement of Jesus' life for our sins ([[Luk 22_20]], [[Mat 26_28]])
	2. 'new covenant in my blood' -> Jesus's death kickstarts the start of a new covenant (Luk 22_20)
	3. "Drink of it, all of you, for this is my blood of the covenant..." ([[Mat 26_27-28]], [[Mark 14_23-24]]) -> Called to drink understanding this represents the new blood, Christ's, that can finally take away the sins of the world once for all ([[Heb 9_28]], [[1 Pet 3_18]]), the better covenant ([[Heb 7_22]])
	4. "I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God" (All the Gospels)-> Thus, the last supper until Jesus's returns and establishes fully the kingdom of God.
4. "For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you **proclaim the Lord 's death until he comes.**" ([[1 Cor 11_26]]) -> Partaking of these 2 items not only for remembrance but for the proclamation of Jesus's death until he comes. I think "Jesus's death until he comes" encompasses the entirety of the Gospel. Who, Why, How, When, What, of it.

>15 And he said to them, "I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. 16 For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God." 17 And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, "Take this, and divide it among yourselves. 18 For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes." 19 And he took **bread**, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, "This is **my body**, which is **given for you**. **Do this in remembrance of me**." 20 And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, "This **cup** that is **poured out for you** is the **new covenant in my blood**.

we see the disciples preparing for the [[Passover]]. And as they were eating it, Jesus tells them what the cup and bread is supposed to point to, what they signified, Jesus's body given and blood poured. Meaning as they continued their [[Passover]] year after year, they were to remember what it signified and pointed to - Christ!

The idea that "Simple Christianity" is what is **sufficient** to understanding the theology of the Gospel. In some level it's true. The Gospel is simple in that it's the "... the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes" ([[Rom 1_16]]), and to whichever degree your theology defines belief as, that is the "Simple Christianity".

However, in the pursuit of maturing in our faith, perhaps it's inaccurate to believe that there's all there is to our faith.

Random reflections that caught my mind as I was reading [[1 Cor 6]]:
The idea that Christians are called to eventually judge angels in v2-3 *"Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases? 3 Do you not know that we are to judge angels?"*. 

This gives the principle that we should have a **desire to move towards wisdom** and discernment in all things because we understand that:
1. Things and Life are not always so black and white, there're grey situations that requires the derivation of higher-order biblical truths.
2. Often times we have incomplete information on the situation and people's heart, yet we have to make a judgment call on what's the maximally godly thing to do, balancing truth, love, grace, holiness, justice, kindness, patience, goodness, etc... the list goes on and on.

Therefore, this would render "Simple Christianity" harder to stand by, as to judge biblically requires "Deep Christianity" that ordinarily requires an emphasis on faithfully pursuing truth and not resting on the usual statements believers make to defend their doctrine: "The Bible says this means this" (Which is true, but it must also be interpreted in light of the rest of Scripture which may give new insight into the original meaning of the verse).

I say this because in [[COC Theology]], there's a tendency to quote bible verses and "let Scripture speak for itself". Which seems to make sense, but it fails to recognise the depth and context of every other single verse in Scripture, which when understood, will reframe how we view those original verses. Particular on the theology of [[Baptism]], [[Women's Prayer]], or [[Musical Instrument]], which I'm more familiar with.

**The Essence of God's Desire for Our Hearts: Life & Truth, Holiness & Love, Grace & Peace**

### Introduction

Understanding God's fundamental nature is crucial for shaping our doctrine and relationship with Him. In Scripture, God's attributes are often revealed in complementary yet contrastive pairs, showing His perfect balance of justice and mercy, holiness and intimacy, truth and love. By examining **Life and Truth, Holiness and Love, and Grace and Peace**, we gain a clearer picture of God's ultimate desire for our hearts as His children.

---

## 1. Life and Truth: The Foundation of Relationship with God

### Life: God's Desire for Eternal Communion

From the beginning, God’s intent for humanity was life—both physical and spiritual. Genesis 2:7 describes how God **breathed life** into Adam, signifying not just biological existence but a deep relational vitality with God (John 17:3).

- Jesus declared, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). True life is not merely existence but is found in **knowing and being in communion with God**.
    
- Eternal life is gifted through Christ (John 3:16), and rejecting Him results in death (Romans 6:23).
    

### Truth: The Nature of God’s Self-Revelation

Truth is inseparable from life because God **is** truth (John 17:17). The Church of Christ often emphasizes obedience to doctrine, but **truth is not just correct doctrine—it is the person of Jesus Christ** (John 14:6).

- Jesus’ confrontation with the Pharisees (John 8:31-32) shows that truth liberates, not enslaves.
    
- Worship must be in **spirit and truth** (John 4:24), meaning it is relational, not just legalistic.
    

Together, **Life and Truth** show that God desires a heart that is **alive in Him and founded upon His self-revealing truth in Christ.**

---

## 2. Holiness and Love: The Balance of Righteousness and Relationship

### Holiness: God's Call to Be Set Apart

God is holy (Isaiah 6:3; 1 Peter 1:16), and He commands His people to be holy.

- Holiness is not just **moral purity** but being **set apart** for God’s purposes (Exodus 19:5-6).
    
- Jesus, the perfect example of holiness, dined with sinners (Mark 2:16-17) **without compromising righteousness.**
    
- True holiness is **not external legalism** but internal transformation (Matthew 23:25-28).
    

### Love: The Driving Force Behind Holiness

Holiness without love can become rigid legalism. God’s holiness does not distance Him from sinners but compels Him to redeem them (Romans 5:8).

- Jesus summarized the Law as **loving God and loving neighbor** (Matthew 22:37-40).
    
- True obedience is **rooted in love, not fear** (1 John 4:18).
    
- The holiness of God led to the cross—where justice and love met perfectly.
    

Together, **Holiness and Love** reveal that God desires a heart that is **set apart for Him yet deeply relational and compassionate.**

---

## 3. Grace and Peace: The Essence of Salvation and Christian Living

### Grace: The Undeserved Favor of God

Grace is foundational to the Gospel (Ephesians 2:8-9). While the Church of Christ often emphasizes **baptism as necessary for salvation**, grace reminds us that salvation is a gift, not a transaction.

- Paul warns against **self-righteousness** (Galatians 2:16) and emphasizes faith in Christ alone.
    
- Even Abraham was justified by faith before any works (Romans 4:3-5).
    
- Grace does not nullify good works but enables them (Titus 2:11-12).
    

### Peace: The Result of Reconciliation with God

Peace is not just the absence of conflict; it is **shalom**, the wholeness that comes from reconciliation with God (Colossians 1:20).

- Justification by faith brings peace with God (Romans 5:1).
    
- The Christian life is marked by peace **not as the world gives, but as Christ gives** (John 14:27).
    
- Legalistic religion robs believers of peace, but grace restores it (Galatians 5:1).
    

Together, **Grace and Peace** show that God desires a heart that is **resting in His unearned favor and living in harmony with Him.**

---

## Conclusion: The Heart God Desires and Its Doctrinal Implications

When we consider these attributes together, we see that God's ultimate desire for our hearts is one that is:

1. **Alive in Christ and rooted in truth** (Life & Truth).
    
2. **Set apart in righteousness yet motivated by love** (Holiness & Love).
    
3. **Secure in grace and walking in peace** (Grace & Peace).
    

This understanding has **profound doctrinal implications**:

- Salvation is not merely about following correct rituals but about **receiving the life, truth, and grace of Christ**.
    
- Legalism without love distorts holiness; **true holiness flows from love**.
    
- Baptism, while important, is not the basis of salvation—**grace is**.
    

Ultimately, the biblical view of God’s desire for our hearts is one of **intimacy, transformation, and assurance in Him.** Any doctrine that places external obedience over internal renewal **misses the heart of God’s desire.**

Love: The Driving Force Behind Holiness

### 1. **Introduction: Baptism and Its Significance**

- **General Overview**: A brief explanation of the centrality of baptism in the New Testament and Christian life.
- **Key Question**: What is the purpose of baptism in Scripture, and how do different forms of baptism—water, Spirit, fire, and into Moses—contribute to the understanding of baptism?

### 2. **Theological Framework: Salvation and Baptism**

- **Biblical Understanding of Salvation**: Examining salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9), and how baptism relates to this understanding.
- **The Church of Christ (COC) View on Baptism**: Overview of COC’s insistence on baptism as essential for salvation, based on passages like Acts 2:38 and Mark 16:16.
- **The Protestant Perspective on Baptism**: Clarifying the distinction between baptism as an act of obedience for believers and baptism’s role in the wider framework of salvation (i.e., faith precedes baptism but baptism is an important response to the gospel).

### 3. **Understanding "Baptizo" in Scripture: The Different Uses**

- **Baptism in Water (Christian Baptism)**:
    
    - The New Testament teaches that baptism in water is a public declaration of faith and union with Christ (Romans 6:3-4, Colossians 2:12).
    - Not a requirement for salvation, but a command from Jesus (Matthew 28:19-20) and the early apostles (Acts 2:38), an outward sign of inner transformation (Acts 22:16).
    - Contrasting COC’s interpretation that baptism is a requirement for forgiveness (cf. Acts 2:38), with the broader Protestant view that baptism follows repentance and faith.
- **Baptism of the Spirit**:
    
    - Explaining Spirit baptism as an instantaneous act of the Holy Spirit at the moment of conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13, Titus 3:5).
    - The Spirit’s baptism is foundational for the believer’s union with Christ and transformation (John 3:5, Romans 8:9). This baptism is not a physical act but a spiritual reality that can only occur through faith in Christ.
    - The contrast: COC emphasizes water baptism as the medium through which one receives the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38), while the Protestant view sees Spirit baptism as the inner work of God that happens simultaneously with faith.
- **Baptism of Fire**:
    
    - Fire baptism is often associated with judgment (Matthew 3:11-12), where John the Baptist speaks of Jesus baptizing with the Holy Spirit and fire. This form of baptism signifies purification and, for the wicked, judgment.
    - In contrast to the "spiritual" baptism by the Spirit (which leads to renewal), baptism by fire emphasizes a future, eschatological judgment.
    - COC may avoid discussing baptism of fire since their focus is on water baptism’s salvific role, but this is important in understanding that baptism is not merely a saving act—it’s part of a broader eschatological story.
- **Baptism into Moses** (1 Corinthians 10:1-2):
    
    - Paul’s reference to baptism into Moses in the context of Israel’s crossing of the Red Sea points to a communal and covenantal aspect of baptism.
    - Baptism here is a symbol of identification with Moses and the covenant God made with Israel, signifying a people’s journey from slavery to freedom.
    - While COC often emphasizes baptism as a personal act for salvation, this “baptism” points to a more communal covenantal symbolism that can help Christians see baptism as part of the larger narrative of redemption through history.

### 4. **Baptism and the Gospel: How Baptism Fits in the Plan of Salvation**

- **The Role of Baptism in the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20)**:
    - Jesus’ command to baptize all nations should be viewed not as a salvific act but as a command to identify believers publicly with the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ.
    - Baptism symbolizes a believer’s participation in Christ’s death and resurrection (Romans 6:3-5).
- **Baptism in Acts**:
    - The Book of Acts shows baptism as the outward sign of repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, Acts 8:36-38). Baptism does not _cause_ salvation but is an important response to faith.
    - **Acts 2:38**: The Church of Christ often points to Acts 2:38 (“Repent and be baptized...for the forgiveness of your sins”) as proof that baptism is essential for salvation. However, the Greek grammar and context indicate that repentance and baptism are both part of the conversion experience, with faith as the foundation (cf. Acts 8:37, 16:31). Baptism signifies repentance and faith, rather than being the means of salvation.
- **Baptism and the New Covenant (Hebrews 10:22-23)**:
    - Baptism, as an act of obedience, points to the New Covenant established by Jesus. It signifies an inward transformation that happens through the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5).
    - The distinction between baptism as a sign of salvation (as some interpret Acts 2:38) and baptism as a covenantal sign (like circumcision in the Old Testament) is key. In this sense, baptism serves as a means of grace, not a saving act in itself.

### 5. **The Historical and Theological Development of Baptism**

- **Church History and Baptism**:
    - The early Church saw baptism as a rite of initiation into the Christian community (Didache 7:1-3). Theologians like Augustine, Martin Luther, and John Calvin emphasized baptism’s importance as a response to grace but did not equate it with the means of salvation.
    - Protestant traditions view baptism as a symbol of the believer’s covenant relationship with God, which follows faith and repentance.
    - **John Calvin** taught that baptism is an outward sign of God’s inward work, while **Luther** stressed baptism’s efficacy but still viewed it as a sign of what God has already done.
- **Theological Contrast**:
    - COC views baptism almost exclusively as the means by which one is saved, citing passages like Acts 2:38, Mark 16:16, and 1 Peter 3:21.
    - Protestantism, while affirming baptism’s importance, emphasizes that salvation comes through faith alone (Ephesians 2:8-9) and that baptism is a public demonstration of an inward faith, not a direct cause of salvation.

### 6. **Practical Application: Pastoral and Ecclesial Concerns**

- **Encouragement to Church of Christ Believers**:
    - While baptism is crucial in the believer's life, it must be seen as part of a broader salvation narrative, not the condition for salvation. This prevents any legalistic view that could distort the gospel message of grace.
- **Encouraging Unity**:
    - The Church of Christ emphasizes the importance of unity in the body of Christ. This is commendable and should be preserved, but understanding baptism within the framework of the Gospel helps avoid division over secondary issues. Unity should be rooted in the message of Christ, not in specific interpretations of baptism.

Here's a comprehensive biblical defense for the use of musical instruments in worship, aimed at engaging a Church of Christ (COC) audience with careful reasoning and biblical references.

---

### **Why It’s Not Biblical to Condemn Musical Instruments in Worship**

The Church of Christ’s stance against musical instruments in worship primarily stems from the belief that the New Testament (NT) does not explicitly authorize them, based on the regulative principle of worship (i.e., "if it's not commanded, it's forbidden"). However, a thorough biblical examination reveals that rejecting musical instruments is not a biblically required position. Instead, Scripture supports their use as a legitimate and God-glorifying expression of worship.

---

## **1. The Old Testament Endorses Musical Instruments in Worship**

The most direct biblical evidence for musical instruments in worship comes from the Old Testament (OT), where God explicitly commanded and endorsed their use in temple worship.

### **A. Instruments Were Divinely Ordained for Worship**

1. **King David and the Temple Musicians**
    
    - _2 Chronicles 29:25_ – _"And he stationed the Levites in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres, according to the commandment of David and of Gad the king’s seer and of Nathan the prophet, for the commandment was from the LORD through his prophets."_
    - The use of instruments was not merely David’s personal preference—it was commanded by God.
2. **Instruments in the Psalms**
    
    - _Psalm 150:3-5_ – _"Praise him with trumpet sound; praise him with lute and harp! Praise him with tambourine and dance; praise him with strings and pipe! Praise him with sounding cymbals; praise him with loud clashing cymbals!"_
    - This is an open command for worshippers to praise God with instruments.
    - Nowhere in the NT does God revoke this form of worship.
3. **Instruments in Prophetic Worship**
    
    - _1 Samuel 10:5_ – _"After that you shall come to Gibeath-elohim, where there is a garrison of the Philistines. And there, as soon as you come to the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre before them, prophesying."_
    - Even the prophets were accompanied by instruments as they prophesied.

### **B. The New Covenant Does Not Repeal the Old Testament’s Teaching on Instruments**

1. **Continuity Between Old and New Covenants**
    
    - Jesus said in _Matthew 5:17_ – _"Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them."_
    - While the sacrificial system was fulfilled in Christ, there is no indication that musical praise was abolished.
2. **Selective Nullification Is Inconsistent**
    
    - Many COC members accept singing from the Psalms (_Ephesians 5:19_, _Colossians 3:16_), yet they reject instruments that are repeatedly endorsed in those very Psalms.
	    - *19 speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord,*
	    - *16 Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.*
    - If Psalm 150’s command to "sing" applies to us, why doesn’t the command to "praise Him with instruments"?

---

## **2. The New Testament Never Forbids Instruments**

A key argument from the COC is that the NT does not explicitly authorize instruments. However, this argument fails for several reasons:

### **A. The Absence of an Explicit Command Does Not Equal Prohibition**

1. **The NT Does Not Mention Many Common Church Practices**
    - The NT does not explicitly command:
        - Church buildings
        - Pews
        - Songbooks
        - Microphones
    - Yet, these are all permitted as expedient aids in worship.
      
2. **Jesus and the Apostles Never Condemn Instruments**
    - If musical instruments were truly sinful, we would expect clear NT prohibitions—yet there are none.
### **B. Early Christian Worship Likely Included Instruments**

1. **Revelation Portrays Heavenly Worship with Instruments**
    - _Revelation 5:8_ – _"And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints."_
    - _Revelation 14:2_ – _"And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps."_
    - If heaven’s worship includes instruments, why would the church on earth be prohibited from using them?
      
2. **The Greek Word for “Make Melody” in Ephesians 5:19 Implies Instruments**
    - _Ephesians 5:19_ – _"Addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart."_
    - The Greek word for "making melody" is _psallō_, which historically meant "to pluck or play a stringed instrument."
    - If Paul had meant to forbid instruments, he would have used a different verb.

---

## **3. The Regulative Principle Is an Unbiblical Restriction**

The COC position assumes the _regulative principle_—that whatever is not commanded is forbidden. However, this principle is not biblically mandated.

1. **The Bible Permits More Than It Commands**
    
    - Colossians 3:17 says, _"Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus."_
    - This allows for practices not explicitly mentioned, so long as they are done for God’s glory.
2. **Jesus Condemns Legalistic Worship Restrictions**
    
    - _Matthew 15:9_ – _"In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men."_
    - Imposing a man-made ban on instruments goes beyond biblical teaching.

---

## **Conclusion: Instruments Are Biblically Permissible and Can Enhance Worship**

- The Old Testament **explicitly commands and celebrates** instrumental worship.
- The New Testament **does not revoke or prohibit** instruments.
- The regulative principle is **not a biblical rule**, and adding restrictions where Scripture does not is legalistic.
- The Book of Revelation presents instruments as **part of heavenly worship**, suggesting their continued use in glorifying God.

Thus, to condemn musical instruments in worship is **not a biblical stance** but rather a human tradition. Instead of focusing on man-made prohibitions, churches should seek to worship God in spirit and truth (_John 4:24_), using every God-given gift to glorify Him—including music.

This is a significant theological issue, and I’ll aim to provide a **biblically faithful, well-reasoned** examination of the role of women in ministry, especially regarding **praying in front of men and leading Bible studies.** Since this is addressed to a **Church of Christ (COC) audience**, I’ll engage with the **common concerns and interpretations** while showing the biblical support for a balanced and faithful view.

---

# **Women’s Role in Ministry: Praying in Front of Men and Leading Bible Studies**

The role of women in ministry is a subject of much debate, particularly in churches that emphasize **male spiritual leadership** based on passages like **1 Timothy 2:12** and **1 Corinthians 14:34-35**. However, a careful examination of **the full biblical witness** reveals that women **played active roles in ministry**, including **prayer and teaching**, and that restrictions must be understood in context.

## **1. Women Praying in Front of Men: Is It Prohibited?**

### **A. 1 Corinthians 11 Shows Women Can Pray in Public**

1 Corinthians 11:5 states:

> _"But every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven."_

This passage indicates that **women were actively praying and prophesying** in a public worship setting. Paul **does not prohibit** women from praying; instead, he gives **instructions on how they should do so** in a way that honors the created order.

### **B. 1 Corinthians 14:34-35: Not a Universal Prohibition on Speaking**

Some argue that **1 Corinthians 14:34-35** forbids women from praying aloud in church:

> _"The women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says."_

However, this must be understood **in context**:

- **Paul had already affirmed that women pray and prophesy (1 Cor 11:5).**
- The **context of chapter 14** is about **order in worship**, not forbidding all speech.
- The **Greek word for “silent” (sigao)** is used earlier in the chapter (14:28, 14:30) to tell **men** to be silent if they lack an interpretation or if someone else is speaking.

### **C. Women Participated in Corporate Prayer in the Early Church**

- **Acts 1:14** – _"All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers."_
    - Women were part of corporate prayer **alongside men** in the early church.
- **Acts 16:13-15** – Lydia and a group of women gathered for prayer, and Paul ministered to them.
- **1 Timothy 2:8-10** – While men are encouraged to pray "lifting holy hands," **women are not excluded** from prayer in any way.

Thus, there is **no biblical basis for prohibiting women from praying in front of men** in church gatherings. Rather, **Paul’s concern is about order and submission to authority, not absolute silence.**

---

## **2. Can Women Lead Bible Studies?**

### **A. Understanding 1 Timothy 2:12 in Context**

A key passage used to prohibit women from teaching is **1 Timothy 2:12**:

> _"I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet."_

However, this verse must be interpreted carefully in light of:

- **Context:** Paul was writing to address false teaching in Ephesus.
- **Key words:** The Greek for "exercise authority" (_authentein_) is rare and may imply **domineering control, not all teaching.**

Since **women like Priscilla (Acts 18:26)** and older women (Titus 2:3-5) clearly taught others, **this passage cannot mean an absolute ban on women teaching**.

### **B. Biblical Examples of Women Teaching**

1. **Priscilla Taught Apollos (Acts 18:26)**
    - Priscilla, alongside her husband Aquila, **taught** the preacher Apollos **correct doctrine**.
    - The text **does not suggest her teaching was improper.
      
2. **Women as Prophets in the Early Church**
    - **Acts 21:9** – Philip’s four daughters **prophesied**, which biblically involves **exhortation, encouragement, and instruction.**
    - **Joel 2:28-29 (fulfilled in Acts 2:17-18)** – God poured out His Spirit on **sons and daughters** to prophesy.
      
3. **Titus 2:3-5 – Older Women Teaching Younger Women**
    - Women **are explicitly commanded** to **teach** younger women, which means teaching is **not inherently forbidden.**
      
4. **Women Were Apostolic Co-Workers**
    - **Romans 16:1-7** lists several women involved in ministry, including **Phoebe (a deacon), Junia (a prominent apostle), and Priscilla (a teacher).**
      

### **C. The Key Issue: Authority, Not Teaching**

The **Bible does not prohibit women from teaching**, but it does place **guardrails on authority** in the church. The real issue in **1 Timothy 2:12** is **exercising authority over men**, which is different from simply leading a Bible study.

- In a **formal church setting**, **elders (who are men) bear responsibility for authoritative teaching (1 Timothy 3:1-7).**
- In **informal or non-authoritative settings**, women **can** teach, lead discussions, and pray (as seen in Acts and the Epistles).

Thus, women leading **a Bible study in a non-authoritative setting** (such as in a **small group, co-ed discussion, or informal teaching**) is **biblically permissible**.

---

## **Conclusion: Biblical Balance on Women's Roles in Ministry**

1. **Women praying in front of men is biblically affirmed** (1 Cor 11:5, Acts 1:14).
2. **Women can teach in various capacities**, provided they do not assume **eldership or domineering authority over men** (Acts 18:26, Titus 2:3-5).
3. **Paul’s restrictions were situational and not absolute prohibitions**, as women in Scripture **prayed, prophesied, and taught** under God’s guidance.

The **Church of Christ's strict interpretation** goes **beyond what the Bible actually teaches**, making a **human rule** into a **divine law**. A **biblical** approach allows **women to serve God faithfully within the framework of biblical order and authority.**

    - Portrays the ambiguities and complexities of life -> Helps us to see how the smaller stories all connect to a big picture (which is exactly what we're going through in our lives today!)
3. **Disadvantages of narratives**
    - Meaning might not be clearly stated.
    - The reader is enthralled by the story and misses meaning.
    - Assume narrative only deals with history, not theology.
    - Read too much theology into narratives.
4. The basic features of plot
    - Exposition: description of the setting
    - Conflict: Can be internal or external
    - Resolution: How the conflict is resolved
    - E.g.
        - Ruth and bethany (house of bread when there's no bread, irony.)
        - The ambiguity whether uriah knew about what King David did. May be the author trying to show us what David himself felt, the ambiguity.
5. Make sure you understand how your episode fits into the book. Min study 3 chapters, before n after.  
6. "Good guys and white hats". Most characters contain a mixture of good n bad traits, don't project this perfection unto them. They're meant to be real people!  
7. God's the main character! Let God be God! Don't bring in theological preconceptions into OT narratives.

**Put On the New Self**
3 If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. 2 Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth. 3 For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. 4 When Christ who is your[a] life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.

12 Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, 13 bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. 14 And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony. 15 And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. 1 Paul, a servant[a] of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, 2 in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began[b] 3 and at the proper time manifested in his word[c] through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;

4 To Titus, my true child in a common faith:

Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.

5 This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— 6 if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife,[d] and his children are believers[e] and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination. 7 For an overseer,[f] as God's steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, 8 but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. 9 He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound[g] doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.

10 For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party.[h] ==11 They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.== 12 One of the Cretans,[i] a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.”[j] 13 This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, 14 not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. 15 To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled. 16 They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.

**Thoughts**
v11: There is a place to "shut down" [[False Doctrine]] for the purpose of being sound in the faith. (v13). The false doctrine Paul refers to are "Jewish myths" and the "commands of people who turn away from the truth".
- What's the truth? Saved only IN Christ, Through Christ, with Christ? (Just got off Colossians, so am heavily influenced by the theme)
- v16, you can tell them by their works.

Devotion reflection: Stand firm in the pure gospel of salvation through Jesus alone! Do not be deceived by liars, test them and see their works. Does the peace of God permeate their life?

>5 Jesus answered, “Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.
>(NKJV)

8-Jul-2025
My reflection when Phoebe asked me about this passage:

To start, John 3:5 is a **complicated** passage, and we have to approach it carefully with **lots of humility and deep reverence for Scripture’s authority**! It’s complicated because there are several strong viewpoints, each with varying strengths and weaknesses. In my reflection, I’ll share my understanding: to be “born of water and the Spirit” in John 3:5 is to believe in Jesus and receive the Holy Spirit, not necessarily to be baptized with water. I’ll explain why, using Scripture, and address other views like baptismal regeneration. Let’s dive in~

## **1. The Theme of Believing in Jesus**

As I read through John, I notice that the theme of believing in Jesus is emphasized over and over again (John 1:12, 50; 2:11, 22; 3:15–16, 18, 36). In John 1:12, it says that to those who believe in His name, Jesus _gives_ the right to become children of God, and in v13, to be **born** nor of flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God -> i.e. To be born of God is to believe in Jesus! **This sets the stage for understanding what it means to be “born again.”**

## **2. Two Baptisms: Water and the Holy Spirit**

We see John the Baptizer baptizing with water for repentance, preparing the way. But there’s another baptism Jesus will do, which seems like the “better baptism”—to be baptized by the _Holy Spirit_ (immersed, poured out). **This distinction is key because it shows that while water baptism is important, the Spirit’s work is central to rebirth.**

## **3. Old Testament Connections**

This reminds me of Ezekiel 36:25–27 and Isaiah 44:2–3, where God promises to pour or sprinkle His Spirit on His children. **These passages link water and the Spirit to cleansing and renewal.** Nicodemus, being a teacher of the law, would’ve known these verses well! **So, when Jesus speaks of being “born of water and the Spirit,” He’s likely drawing on these promises that Nicodemus should recognize.**

## **4. Jesus’ Challenge to Nicodemus**

Building on this, Jesus challenges Nicodemus’ understanding in John 3:3 and 3:10, asking what it truly means to be “born again.” He answers while staying consistent with God’s Word from the past. In John 3:15, 16, 18, and 36, it’s clear: whoever believes in Jesus shall not perish but have everlasting life. **So, to be “born again of water and the Spirit” is tied to believing in Jesus.**

## **5. Born of God, Not of Flesh**

John 1:13 and John 3:6 repeat the idea that those who believe in Jesus are born not of flesh, but of God. To be born of God is to be baptized with the Holy Spirit, and this must involve cleansing because God cannot dwell in sin. **That’s why Ezekiel and Isaiah make sense here—they promise both cleansing and the Spirit.**

**So, to be “born of water and the Spirit” means being baptized with the Holy Spirit through believing in Jesus, as John keeps emphasizing.**

## **Other Views: Baptismal Regeneration**

Could baptism be necessary to be “born again of water and the Spirit”? It could be, as many early church fathers supported baptismal regeneration (BR). **In fact, passages like Acts 2:38 and Mark 16:16 seem to link baptism with salvation, and early Christians often saw baptism as the means of regeneration.** This is strong evidence for BR, but I believe Scripture should take supreme authority over tradition.

**Here’s why I differ:** The rest of the Bible shows we are saved by grace through faith (alone), not by works, lest we boast (Ephesians 2:8–9). Baptism in Acts and elsewhere is a powerful symbol of repentance and proclamation of Christ, but justification comes from faith in Jesus (alone). For example, the thief on the cross was saved without baptism (Luke 23:40–43), and Romans 4 teaches that faith, not works like circumcision, justifies us. **Similarly, baptism is a _necessary_ picture of our faith, just as circumcision was for Israel, but it’s not what saves us.**

**So, passages like John 3:5, Acts 2:38, and Mark 16:16 must be understood in light of the whole Bible, which emphasizes faith for salvation.**

## **Conclusion**

**In humility, I see John 3:5 as spiritual rebirth through faith in Jesus, receiving the Holy Spirit (John 1:12, Ezekiel 36). Baptism pictures this, but faith saves.** We are baptized today in obedience to Jesus’ command (Matthew 28:19), not for salvation (Colossians 3, Romans 4), but as a symbol of being in Christ’s saving work (Galatians 3:26–27, Colossians 2:11–13, Romans 6:4).

Once again, I recognize that I’m a finite sinner, and there could be inaccuracies! But this view makes sense to me, and I’m convicted of it. I’m open to probing questions as I continue learning!
headings: **1. The Theme of Believing in Jesus**
**2. Two Baptisms: Water and the Holy Spirit**
**5. Born of God, Not of Flesh**

My reflections:
A jew is not one who does outward actions but rather by the state of his internal "actions", his heart!

Therefore, someone who does the outward act of circumcision is still not a "jew" unless his heart is also circumcised! And circumcision DOES NOT happen by man's decision to follow the letter of the law (29), but by God's Spirit!! And therefore, the praise shouldn't go to congratulating the man who decided to be circumcised, but to God who did the circumcision of the heart!

Replace circumcision with baptism and you start to see a lot of similarities. Help us God to understand!

nodes.content:
# Scripture
### The Example of Christ

15 We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. 2 Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up. 3 For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.” 4 For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. 5 May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus, 6 that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. 7 Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.

### Christ the Hope of Jews and Gentiles

8 For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God's truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, 9 and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written,

“Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles,  
    and sing to your name.”

10 And again it is said,

“Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people.”

11 And again,

“Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles,  
    and let all the peoples extol him.”

12 And again Isaiah says,

“The root of Jesse will come,  
    even he who arises to rule the Gentiles;  
in him will the Gentiles hope.”

13 May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.

### Paul the Minister to the Gentiles

14 I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers,[[a](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans%2015&version=ESV#fen-ESV-28302a "See footnote a")] that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. 15 But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God 16 to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. 17 In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God. 18 For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience—by word and deed, 19 by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God—so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ; 20 and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else's foundation, 21 but as it is written,

“Those who have never been told of him will see,  
    and those who have never heard will understand.”

### Paul's Plan to Visit Rome

22 This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. 23 But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you, 24 I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while. 25 At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. 26 For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem. 27 For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings. 28 When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected,[[b](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans%2015&version=ESV#fen-ESV-28316b "See footnote b")] I will leave for Spain by way of you. 29 I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing[[c](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans%2015&version=ESV#fen-ESV-28317c "See footnote c")] of Christ.

30 I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, 31 that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints, 32 so that by God's will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. 33 May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

nodes.content:
Greeting
1 Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,

2 To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours:

3 Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Thanksgiving
4 I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, 5 that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge— 6 even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— 7 so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ, 8 who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Divisions in the Church
10 I appeal to you, brothers,[a] by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. 11 For it has been reported to me by Chloe's people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers. 12 What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” 13 Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? 14 I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, 15 so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. 16 (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.) 17 For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.

Christ the Wisdom and Power of God
18 For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. 19 For it is written,

“I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,
    and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”

20 Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? 21 For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach[b] to save those who believe. 22 For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, 23 but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, 24 but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. 25 For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

26 For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards,[c] not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. 27 But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong; 28 God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, 29 so that no human being[d] might boast in the presence of God. 30 And because of him[e] you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption, 31 so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
